title: Ang 1364–1370: Kabir's saloks, first half
hookLine: I am the worst of all, the Lord's dog
tomorrow: Kabir names where the Lord is. it isn't a place. what is it?

cards: Every feed says the same thing in a thousand ways: you're the main character. On ang 1364 Kabir flips it. In paraphrase: Kabir, I'm the worst of all; everyone else is good.

A few pages on, at ang 1368, he goes further. Kabir is the Lord's dog, Moti's my name; there's a chain around my neck, and wherever I'm pulled, I go. So, today's question: is that low self-esteem, or something else?

teach.h: THE HALF PEOPLE SKIP: ALL ELSE GOOD.
teach.b: Start with the half people skip. Kabir doesn't only call himself the worst. He says everyone else is good, and in paraphrase: whoever understands it this way is my friend.
That isn't self-hatred. It's a way of looking: at other people first, for their goodness, before your own. The dog says the same from another side.

teach.h: THE DOG IS HELD, NOT ASHAMED.
teach.b: A dog on a chain isn't ashamed of it. It's held. It goes where its person goes, and it trusts the hand.
Kabir picks a humble animal of the house and wears it like a name tag. His isn't the only voice like this.

teach.h: PAUL: OF WHOM I AM CHIEF.
teach.b: In the Christian New Testament, Paul writes: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.” Two voices, worlds apart, putting themselves at the bottom of the list.
What they share: the lowest place isn't a wound. It's where each stands to look up at something greater. And one honest difference.
Paul says it about Christ, who in his faith saves sinners, and he rests it there.
Kabir names no savior figure. He rests on the Lord's chain, and on seeing everyone else as good. Neither is the other.

how: Kabir's saloks are read in the Granth's closing pages; Sikhs quote 'I am the worst of all, everyone else is good' as a picture of humility, and read his couplets in sehaj path and talks.

games.q: Kabir's couplets, ang 1364–1370 — tap the pairs.
p: the dog's name, on a chain

s: Kabir's couplet teaches people to hate themselves
its other half is: everyone else is good. it's a way of looking for others' goodness first.
Kabir calls himself the Lord's dog, with a chain around his neck
and wherever he's pulled, he goes. held, not ashamed.
Kabir's line and Paul's line mean exactly the same thing
both bow low; Paul rests it on Christ who saves, Kabir on the Lord's chain and on seeing others as good.

games.q: Maya says her grandmother's favorite verse is Paul calling himself chief of sinners, and asks if Kabir means the same. what's the fair answer?
o: both put themselves lowest; Paul rests it on Christ who saves, Kabir on the Lord's chain.
yes, it's the exact same teaching, just in two languages with two names.
no, they have nothing in common at all; one's Christian and one isn't.
games.why: something shared, honestly told, and something different, honestly told. neither is ranked, and neither is folded into the other.

practice: Let your head bow a little, chin toward your chest, the shape of someone at the bottom of the list, and breathe there through the sit. If a face comes to mind, let it come with one good thing about them.
